title: Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–40)
hook: an African official reads Isaiah in his chariot and asks, what hinders me?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen, remembered as the first martyr, a witness to the end. Your line was lay not this sin to their charge. Did you loosen your grip on one grudge? Day seventy-nine.
screen: `LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Ever been stuck on a page? A contract, a tax form, a poem for school, a medicine label. You read it three times and the words just sit there. Now go to a desert road running south from Jerusalem toward Gaza. A chariot is rolling along, carrying a very important man: the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, a court official in charge of all her wealth. He's been to Jerusalem to worship, a long trip from Africa, and now, heading home, he's reading a scroll of the prophet Isaiah out loud. And he's stuck. Meanwhile an angel has told Philip, one of the seven food organizers, to go and stand on that road. Just that. Go and stand there.
screen: `STUCK ON A PAGE.` → `A CHARIOT ON THE DESERT ROAD.` → `GO AND STAND THERE.`

segments.voice: The Spirit tells Philip to go up to the chariot, so he runs alongside it and hears the man reading. And he asks, in the King James Bible: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The official's answer is plain: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" He invites Philip up. The passage is Isaiah's song of the suffering servant: led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent, humiliated. Who is the prophet talking about, the man asks, himself or someone else? And Philip, starting from that page, tells him about Jesus. There's something else in the background. The official is called a eunuch, and Deuteronomy says a eunuch may not enter the assembly of the Lord. But a few chapters further on in the very scroll he's holding, God promises eunuchs who keep his covenant a place, and a name that will never be cut off. Whether he'd read that far, the text doesn't say. Then they pass some water by the road, and he asks the question of the day: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" What's stopping me? In the King James text, Philip's only condition is that he believe with all his heart. Then they stop the chariot, go down into the water, and he's baptized. Philip is suddenly gone, and the official goes on his way rejoicing. Scholars think the Ethiopia of Acts was the kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in what's now Sudan. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church treasures the story all the same. And some readers hear in it a quiet echo of Pentecost: the good news heading out toward the ends of the earth, one reader at a time.
screen: `UNDERSTANDEST THOU WHAT THOU READEST?` · `HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?` · `A PLACE PROMISED IN ISAIAH.` · `WHAT DOTH HINDER ME?` · then, large: `HE WENT ON HIS WAY REJOICING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain something kindly to someone. Sit, and breathe. Think of someone who's stuck on something you understand. A kid with homework, a parent with a phone, a new coworker, a friend with a form. Notice how Philip does it. He runs to catch up. He asks a question first. He starts from the exact page they're on, not from where he'd like to start. Picture doing that, gently, without a sigh. If you pray, you can pray for that person. The bell holds the time.
Eunuch. The title Acts gives the Ethiopian official, a man the law once excluded, who Philip baptizes anyway, right there by the road.
Your line: what hinders you? Today, help one person with one page, starting where they are. Tomorrow, the young man who held the coats meets a light on the road. Day seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Christians often read the story of Philip and the Ethiopian as a picture of the good news reaching Africa and of baptism welcoming someone once kept at the edge. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church holds the story especially dear.

original.note: Greek: hinders, prevents. The official's question is ti kolyei me: what hinders me?

trapdoor: what you thought: a missionary story.
what it means: a man stuck on a hard page asks for help, gets it, and asks the day's question: what hinders me? nothing stands in his way.
what a scholar hears: Ethiopia meant Kush, the official was a eunuch once kept at the edge of the assembly, and Isaiah 56 promises eunuchs a lasting name.

notes: Acts 8:37 (the confession) is absent from many early manuscripts; the script skips from the question to the baptism.
Ethiopia = Kush/Meroë in ancient usage; 'Candace' is a royal title (kandake). The script says 'the queen of the Ethiopians' and does not name her.
The link to Isaiah 56:3–5 and Deuteronomy 23:1 is offered as background; the script says the text doesn't tell us whether he had read Isaiah 56.
Whether 'eunuch' is literal or a court title is debated; the script treats it as the text presents it. Confirm.
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's attachment to this story: confirm wording.

Review (days 76–93 editor pass, 2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the script said 'Philip's answer is: nothing', but the KJV it quotes has Philip answer with a condition (Acts 8:37, 'If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest'), now reflected; the verse is absent from many early manuscripts, so a Keeper may prefer to drop it. Also: 'the old law' (supersessionist ring) now names Deuteronomy; cut the generalization that ancient people read aloud; Kush identification now 'scholars think'; cut 'one of the oldest churches in the world'; 'many Christians' now 'some readers'; hook's 'Now picture' replaced.
